COTTONWOOD HEIGHTS CITY
PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING AGENDA
July 1, 2026
Notice is hereby given that the Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission will convene on Wednesday, July 1,
2026, at Cottonwood Heights City Hall (2277 E. Bengal Blvd., Cottonwood Heights, UT 84121) for its Work
Session and Business Session meetings.

   1. Work Session – 5:00 p.m. –Council workroom
   2. Business Session – 6:00 p.m. – City Council Chambers

Both sessions will also be broadcast electronically on the city’s YouTube channel at
https://www.youtube.com/@CottonwoodHeights/streams.
Please see the reverse side of this agenda for instructions on how to make public comments.

5:00 p.m. Work Session
       1.0 Welcome new Planning Commission member

       2.0 Review Business Session Agenda
       The commission will review and discuss agenda items.

       3.0 CUP-25-005 -Old Mill Demolition

       4.0 Adjourn

6:00 p.m. Business Session
       1.0 Welcome and Acknowledgements
              1.1 Ex parte communications or conflicts of interest to disclose.

       2.0 General Public Comment
       This is an opportunity for individuals to make general public comments that do not relate to any projects
       scheduled for public hearing under the “Business Items” section of this agenda. Please see the Public
       Comment Policy on the reverse side of this agenda for more information.

       3.0 Business Items

               3.1 Project SUB-26-004
               The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to review a request for Preliminary Plat approval
               for the Ivory Bengal Blvd & 2300 East Subdivision, a proposed 10-lot single-family residential
               subdivision located at 2327 E. Bengal Boulevard. The proposal includes ten (10) residential lots, one
               stormwater detention parcel, a new public street, and associated public improvements within the R-
               1-8 Residential Single-Family Zone.

               3.2 Project ZTA-26-002
               The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing and make a possible recommendation to the
               City Council on a city-initiated request for a Zoning Text Amendment to modify CHMC Chapter
               19.34 regarding development standards in the RM (Residential Multi-Family) zone, and
               corresponding definitions in CHMC Chapter 19.04

       4.0 Consent Agenda
              4.1 Approval of June 3, 2026, Planning Commission Minutes.
       5.0 Adjourn
       Next Planning Commission Meeting: August 5, 2026.

Public Comment
Individuals may provide public comments verbally or via writing.

Verbal comments are accepted in person at the 6:00 p.m. Business Session, but not at the 5:00 p.m. Work
Session. At the Business Session, public comments may be given during two intervals:
   1. General Public Comment Period – An opportunity for general comments not relating to specific projects on
       the meeting agenda.
   2. Specific Project Public Hearings – An opportunity for comments relating to specific projects on the meeting
       agenda which were noticed as public hearings.
Please note that verbal comments must be provided by attending the meetings in-person. Verbal comments
cannot be provided via the electronic broadcast of planning commission meetings on the city’s YouTube channel.

Verbal comment periods are an opportunity for individuals to share comments as they see fit but are not an
opportunity for “question and answer” dialogue. Questions should be directed to city staff at
planning@ch.utah.gov. Verbal comments provided during the public comment period will be limited to three
minutes per individual, or five minutes per a spokesperson who has been asked by a group that is present to
summarize their concerns.

Alternatively, written comments may be submitted to staff via email at planning@ch.utah.gov. For written
comments to be entered into the record and distributed to the planning commission prior to the meeting, they must
be submitted to staff by 12:00 p.m. MDT on Tuesday, June 30, 2026, the day prior to the meeting. Comments
received after this deadline will be distributed to the planning commission after the meeting.

Meeting Procedures
Items will generally be considered in the following order: 1. Chair introduction of item, 2. Staff presentation, 3.
Applicant presentation, if applicable, 4. Chair opens public hearing, if applicable, 5. Chair closes public hearing, if
applicable, 6. Planning commission deliberation, 7. Planning commission motion and vote on item.

Applications may be tabled if additional information is needed in order to act on the item; or if the planning
commission feels there are unresolved issues that may need further attention before the commission is ready
to make a motion. No agenda item will begin after 9:00 pm without a unanimous vote of the commission. The
commission may carry over agenda items, scheduled late in the evening and not heard, to the next regularly
scheduled meeting.

Notice of Compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, individuals needing special accommodations or
assistance during this meeting shall notify the City Recorder at (801) 944-7015 at least 24 hours prior to the
meeting. TDD number is (801) 270-2425 or call Relay Utah at #711.

Confirmation of Public Notice
On Thursday, June 25, 2026, a copy of the foregoing notice was posted in conspicuous view in the front foyer
of the Cottonwood Heights City Offices. The agenda was also posted on the City’s website at
www.cottonwoodheights.utah.gov and the Utah public notice website at http://pmn.utah.gov.

Context

Church of Jesus

Acreage:
3.2 acres


Request
The applicant is requesting approval of a preliminary plat for the “Ivory Bengal Blvd & 2300 East
Subdivision,” a proposed 10-lot single-family detached residential subdivision located within the R-
1-8 Residential Single-Family Zone.
The subject property is currently developed with an existing LDS church meetinghouse and
associated parking facilities. The existing structures and associated site improvements are
proposed to be demolished.

Summary/Background
According to the applicant’s narrative, the proposed subdivision is intended to redevelop the existing
church property into a low-density residential neighborhood consistent with the existing zoning
designation and General Plan land use designation.
                                                            Planning Commission – July 1, 2026
                                                      Project SUB-26-004 – 2327 E. Bengal Blvd.

The subject property is currently owned by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The
applicant, Ivory Homes, is currently under contract with the property owner.
Staff finds that redevelopment of the existing institutional property into a detached single-family
residential subdivision is generally compatible with the surrounding residential neighborhood,
existing development pattern, and the underlying R-1-8 zoning designation.
The proposed subdivision is intended solely for permitted residential uses, including:
   •   Single-family detached dwellings; and
   •   Accessory structures customary to single-family residential use.

The subject property contains approximately 3.2 gross acres. The project proposes dedication of
approximately 0.55 acres as public right-of-way associated with the new internal roadway, resulting
in approximately 2.47 net acres of private residential property.
The proposed subdivision density is approximately 3.3 dwelling units per acre.

Applicable Code
Subdivision Regulations

The subdivision is subject to the requirements of Title 12 (Subdivisions) of the Cottonwood Heights
Municipal Code.

Zoning Regulations

The property is located within the R-1-8 Residential Single-Family Zone regulated under Chapter
19.26 of the Cottonwood Heights Municipal Code.

The purpose of the R-1-8 zone is to provide for low-density detached residential development
compatible with surrounding suburban neighborhoods.

Analysis
Zoning Compliance and Density

The applicant proposes a 10-lot single-family residential subdivision consistent with the permitted
uses of the R-1-8 zone.

The proposed subdivision density of approximately 3.3 dwelling units per acre is generally
compatible with the surrounding neighborhood and consistent with the intended development
pattern of the R-1-8 zone.

Lot Mix Summary

 Standard                      Proposed                       Code Requirement

 Total Number of Lots          10                             N/A

 Minimum Lot Width             81.04 feet                     70’ at 20’ from front lot line

 Minimum Lot Depth             97.30 feet                     N/A

 Minimum Lot Area              8,705 square feet              8,000 square feet

 Largest Lot Area              Approx. 17,130 square feet     N/A

 Parcel A/Detention            2,925 square feet

Staff finds the proposed subdivision complies with the dimensional requirements of the R-1-8 zone,
including minimum lot width and minimum lot area requirements.



Subdivision Design and Layout

The proposed subdivision is organized around a new internal public roadway identified as “Street A.”
The roadway section includes:

   •   A 56-foot public right-of-way
   •   Sidewalks on both sides of the street

                                                                                           Page 3 of 7
                                                            Planning Commission – July 1, 2026
                                                      Project SUB-26-004 – 2327 E. Bengal Blvd.

    •   Park strips; and
    •   Curb and gutter improvements.

The proposed lot arrangement and subdivision layout are generally compatible with the surrounding
residential subdivision pattern and provide orderly residential development of the site.

The existing church building, parking areas, sidewalks, landscaping, utilities, and associated site
improvements are proposed to be removed as part of the redevelopment.




Traffic and Access

Access to the subdivision is proposed from Bengal Boulevard through a single access point located
along the southern portion of the property.

At the request of the City Engineering Department, the applicant submitted a traffic study evaluating
the proposed subdivision and access configuration. The traffic study prepared by Focus Consulting
evaluated existing roadway conditions, projected trip generation, and access operations.

Existing Roadway Conditions

The traffic study identifies:

    •   Bengal Boulevard as an urban collector roadway with one travel lane in each direction and a
        center two-way left-turn lane
    •   2300 East as an urban collector roadway with one northbound and one southbound lane;
        and
    •   Posted speeds of 35 mph on both roadways.

Trip Generation

Using ITE Land Use Code 210 (Single-Family Detached Housing), the study estimates the proposed
subdivision will generate:

    •   Approximately 94 average daily trips (ADT)
    •   7, AM peak hour trips
    •   9, PM peak hour trips

The study concludes the proposed subdivision would have minimal impact on surrounding roadway
operations and that the proposed access location is appropriate for the anticipated traffic volumes
associated with the development.

Staff and the City Engineer reviewed the submitted traffic study and find the proposed access
configuration acceptable, subject to standard engineering review and approval.




                                                                                         Page 4 of 7
                                                             Planning Commission – July 1, 2026
                                                       Project SUB-26-004 – 2327 E. Bengal Blvd.

Utilities and Infrastructure

The subdivision proposes installation of new water, sewer, storm drainage, roadway, sidewalk, and
utility infrastructure necessary to serve the proposed lots. Final engineering plans and utility plans
will be reviewed by the City Engineer prior to final plat approval and recordation.



Stormwater and Detention

The proposed subdivision includes an on-site stormwater detention system located within Parcel A.
The grading and drainage plans identify a detention pond with approximately 3,836 cubic feet of
provided storage volume intended to accommodate stormwater runoff generated by the
development.

Parcel A, including all stormwater detention facilities and associated common area improvements,
will be privately owned and maintained by the subdivision’s homeowner’s association (HOA).
Maintenance obligations will be identified within the project CC&Rs and HOA documents prior to
final plat recordation.

Staff finds the proposed stormwater detention facilities are sufficient for preliminary review
purposes, subject to final engineering review and approval by the City Engineer.



Comments from Other City Departments

The Public Works Department and Unified Fire Authority have both conducted a preliminary review
of the proposed project. (Additional technical review will continue through the final engineering and
final plat review process.). To date the review comments include:

   •   The City Engineer reviewed the preliminary plat and traffic statement. The applicant
       submitted revised plans addressing engineering review comments. Any remaining technical
       corrections shall be addressed prior to final plat approval; and

   •   Provide storm drain design details and calculations.

Staff finds these preliminary comments can be appropriately addressed during the final plat
process. Should addressing these comments affect approval issued by the Planning Commission,
the applicant may be required to return to Planning Commission for approval of the revised project.

Planning Commission Authority
The Planning Commission is the approval authority for administrative applications, including
preliminary plat approval requested by this application. The details of such authority are included
below:

Following a review of the preliminary plat by the Planning Commission, the Community Development
Department and other interested city departments, the Planning Commission shall act on the plat
as submitted or modified. (12.12.030)


                                                                                           Page 5 of 7
                                                             Planning Commission – July 1, 2026
                                                       Project SUB-26-004 – 2327 E. Bengal Blvd.

Findings
Findings of fact include:
   1. The proposed subdivision complies with the applicable requirements of Title 12
      (Subdivisions) of the Cottonwood Heights Municipal Code, subject to the recommended
      conditions of approval.
   2. The proposed subdivision complies with the applicable dimensional and use requirements
      of the R-1-8 Residential Single-Family Zone, including minimum lot area, minimum lot width,
      and permitted residential uses.
   3. The R-1-8 zoning district permits a theoretical density of approximately 5.45 dwelling units
      per acre. The proposed subdivision density is approximately 3.3 dwelling units per acre.
   4. The proposed subdivision layout provides for orderly residential development and includes
      lots, streets, drainage facilities, utilities, and public improvements generally consistent with
      City subdivision standards.
   5. The proposed subdivision provides adequate access from Bengal Boulevard, and the
      submitted traffic analysis demonstrates the proposed access location will not create
      significant traffic impacts to the surrounding roadway network.
   6. The proposed stormwater detention and drainage facilities, including the detention pond
      located within Parcel A, appear adequate for preliminary plat review purposes subject to final
      engineering review and approval.
   7. Unified Fire Authority reviewed and approved the proposed subdivision on June 15, 2026.
If approved by the Planning Commission, this application will undergo a full technical review for
compliance with all city standards prior to final plat approval and recordation. Technical correction
items will be identified in this review and provided to the applicant.

Recommended Conditions of Approval
   1. The development shall substantially conform to the approved preliminary plat and
      supporting application materials.
   2. All applicable requirements of Title 12 and Title 19 of the Cottonwood Heights Municipal
      Code shall be satisfied prior to final plat approval.
   3. Final engineering plans, utility plans, drainage plans, and public improvement plans shall be
      reviewed and approved by the City and referral agencies prior to final plat approval.
   4. All roadway, sidewalk, drainage, utility, landscaping, and public infrastructure improvements
      shall be installed or financially guaranteed prior to final plat recordation.
   5. The applicant shall comply with all requirements of the City Engineer, utility providers,
      Unified Fire Authority, and all other applicable reviewing agencies.
   6. Any necessary easements shall be dedicated and recorded with the final plat.
   7. Parcel A, including all stormwater detention facilities, drainage improvements, landscaping,
      and associated common area improvements, shall be privately owned and maintained by
      the homeowners association (HOA). Appropriate maintenance obligations shall be
      incorporated into the project CC&Rs and HOA documents prior to final plat recordation.
   8. The final plat shall be recorded within one (1) year of preliminary plat approval unless an
      extension is granted in accordance with Chapter 12 of the Cottonwood Heights Municipal
      Code.

COTTONWOOD HEIGHTS CITY
PLANNING COMMISSION
STAFF MEMO
July 1, 2026

Summary
This is a city-initiated request for a zoning text amendment to update standards in the Cottonwood
Heights Municipal Code (CHMC) Chapter 19.34: RM – Residential Multi-Family Zone. The proposed
amendments are intended to:
   •    Clarify existing development standards,
   •    Remove unintended regulatory barriers to townhouse development,
   •    Improve internal consistency of dimensional standards, and
   •    Clarify when a Master Development Plan is required.

Staff Analysis
The proposed amendments are intended to improve the functionality and clarity of the RM zoning
district by removing unnecessary regulatory barriers while maintaining compatibility with
surrounding development. The changes are expected to make townhouse development more
feasible by allowing more efficient site design and providing clear, objective standards for setbacks
and lot width.
Clarifying that shared party walls are exempt from interior side setbacks and exempting townhouses
from the minimum lot width requirement will reduce ambiguity during project review and create
greater predictability for applicants and staff. The reduction in the front setback from 30 feet to 20
feet is consistent with the goal of improving site efficiency without altering existing standards for
building height, lot coverage, or open space. Additionally, clarifying that permitted uses are not
subject to the Master Development Plan process eliminates an unnecessary discretionary review
requirement for by-right development.

Overall, staff finds that the proposed amendments are consistent with the purpose of the RM zoning
district and recommends that the Planning Commission forward a recommendation of approval to
the City Council for adoption of the proposed text amendments.

14   19.34.010 Purpose Of Chapter
15   The purpose of the RM zone is to provide areas in the city for high-density residential
16   development.

17   19.34.020 Permitted Uses
18   Permitted uses in the RM zone are as follows:
19   A. Single-family dwellings, attached or detached;
20   B. Accessory buildings customary to multi-family and single-family residential buildings;
21      and
22   C. Home occupations.
23
24   19.34.030 Conditional Uses
25   Conditional uses in the RM zone are as follows:
26   A. Bed and breakfast;
27   B. Churches;
28   C. Day care/pre-school, as allowed by the applicable accessory regulations in Chapter
29      19.76, “Supplementary and Qualifying Regulations”;
30   D. Dwelling group, provided that;
31      1. The parcel of ground on which the dwelling group (as defined in Chapter 19.04,
32         “Definitions”) is to be erected shall have an area equal to the aggregate of the
33         minimum lot areas otherwise required in the zone for the number of individual
34         dwelling structures in the group.
35      2. The distance between principal buildings shall be equal to the total side yards
36         required in the zone. The distance between principal buildings and the nearest
37         perimeter lot line shall be at least 15 feet. The distance between any building and a
38         public street shall be at least the front yard required in the zoning district, except on
39         corner lots the side yard which faces on a public street shall be at least 20 feet.
40      3. Access shall be provided by a private street or right-of-way from a public street; such
41         private street or right-of-way shall be at least 20 feet wide for one or two rear
42         dwelling units and at least 30 feet wide for three or more dwelling units.
43      4. A minimum of two parking spaces shall be provided for each dwelling unit. Parking
44         spaces and vehicular maneuvering areas shall meet city standards.
45      5. Every dwelling structure in the dwelling group shall be within 60 feet of an access

                                                                                             Page 1 of 3
46         roadway or drive.
47      6. The development plan shall provide a buffer landscaped area along all property lines
48         and decorative landscaping adjacent to the buildings in appropriate locations. Solid
49         visual fences shall be provided along all interior property lines unless the planning
50         commission approves otherwise.
51   E. Golf course;
52   F. Hospital;
53   G. Hotel;
54   H. Lodging house;
55   I. Multiple unit dwellings, either apartments or condominiums;
56   J. Nursing home;
57   K. Offices, professions and general business;
58   L. Planned unit development;
59   M. Private parks and recreational grounds;
60   N. Public and quasi-public use;
61   O. Radio and/or television tower;
62   P. Temporary structures, as allowed by the applicable accessory regulations in Chapter
63      19.76, “Supplementary and Qualifying Regulations”;
64   Q. Two-family dwellings;
65   R. Utility stations and lines, as allowed by the applicable accessory regulations in Chapter
66      19.76, “Supplementary and Qualifying Regulations”; and
67   S. Public schools.
68
69   19.34.040 Minimum Lot Size
70   The minimum lot size in the RM zone is 10,000 square feet for each single-family or
71   two-family dwelling, with 2,000 extra square feet for each additional unit in a building with
72   more than one unit.

73   19.34.050 Minimum Lot Width
74   The minimum lot width in the RM zone is 65 feet measured 30 20 feet from the front lot line.
75   This standard does not apply to attached single-family dwellings (townhouses).

76   19.34.060 Setbacks/Yard Requirements
77
78   A. Setbacks/yard requirements are intended to provide a description of the required space
79      between buildings and property lines. Primary buildings shall maintain a minimum
80      distance from property lines as follows:
81      Front: 30 20 feet.
82      Sides: On interior lots, a total of at least 25 feet between the two side yards, with no side
83      yard of less than ten 10 feet. On corner lots, at least 30 20 feet on the street side and at least
84      10 feet on the interior side.
85      Side Setback for Single-Family, Attached (Townhouse): Townhouses with a shared party
86      wall are exempt from the interior side setback requirement along the shared wall. End units
87      shall maintain a minimum 10-foot setback from the exterior side property line. On corner
88      lots, end units shall maintain a minimum 20-foot setback from the street side property line.
89      Rear: 30 feet.

                                                                                                Page 2 of 3
90
91    B. Accessory buildings in the RM zone shall maintain a minimum distance from property
92       lines as follows:
93       Front: Accessory buildings, excluding garages, shall maintain a setback of at least six feet
94       from primary buildings in the rear yard for the particular property.
95       Sides: Five feet, excluding garages, on interior lots; 20 feet on street side of corner lots.
96       Rear: Five feet, excluding garages, on interior lots; 20 feet on corner lots. Attached garages
97       shall conform to the rear yard requirements of main buildings. Detached garages shall
98       conform to the rear yard requirements of accessory buildings, provided that the garage is in
99       the rear yard and at least six feet away from the main building.
100      Garages: The minimum side yard for a private garage shall be eight feet, except that private
101      garages and other accessory buildings located in the rear yard and at least six feet away
102      from the primary building shall maintain a minimum side yard of not less than five feet.
103
104   HISTORY
105   Amended by Ord. 429 on 1/7/2025

106   19.34.070 Maximum Height Of Structures
107
108   A. For uses where the slope of the original ground surface is greater than 15%, or if a slope
109      stability hazard is present on site, the maximum structure height shall be 30 feet.
110   B. All other properties shall maintain a maximum structure height of 35 feet.
111   C. Accessory Buildings.
112      No accessory building shall exceed 20 feet in height. For each foot of height over 14 feet,
113      accessory buildings shall be set back from property lines an additional foot from the
114      minimum setback to allow a maximum height of 20 feet.
115
116   HISTORY
117   Amended by Ord. 412 on 4/9/2024

118   19.34.080 Maximum Lot Coverage
119   The maximum lot coverage in the RM zone is 50%, including all structures, except portions of
120   those properties also located in the Sensitive Lands Overlay Zone, for which the maximum lot
121   coverage shall be 30% including all structures and impervious surfaces.
122   HISTORY
123   Amended by Ord. 412 on 4/9/2024

125   The minimum open space requirement for developments over two acres in the RM zone is
126   15%.

127   19.34.100 Master Development Plan Required
128   Except for permitted land uses listed in Section 19.34.020, Any development of land in the
129   RM zone shall be subject to the requirements of a master development plan approved by the
130   planning commission.

WORK SESSION

Chair Sean Steinman called the Planning Commission Work Session to order at 4:32 p.m. He thanked
Commissioner Anderson and Commissioner Mills for their service over the last two terms.

1.0    Review Business Session Agenda.

Chair Steinman reviewed the Business Session Agenda and reported that the Business Items would
be discussed later in the meeting.

2.0    CUP-25-005 – Old Mill Demolition.

Community and Economic Development Director, Jim Spung, provided updates on the project. The
applicant deferred the June submittal to July, so there were no new materials for review.

The five companies that responded to the Request for Qualifications (“RFQ”) had been interviewed,
and the City Council was scheduled to approve Dunn Associates as the project consultant. All the
submittals were excellent, but they stood out as having the best qualifications for the project. Mr.
Spung hoped that the report would be available by August 31.

In response to a question raised by Commissioner Barnes, Mr. Spung reported that negotiations were
still in process, but the total cost would be below the original $20,000 estimate. Costs would likely
be applied to the current-year budget.

Commissioner Mills asked if the consultant was local. Mr. Spung reported that the owner of the firm
lives in Cottonwood Heights near the Old Mill. That was not a requirement, but it was beneficial.
Chair Steinman stated that Dunn Associates worked on many historical buildings in downtown Salt
Lake City, including their own building, which was the original granary in the granary district.



Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                          1
Mr. Spung reported the consultant would present their findings to the Planning Commission in
September or October 2026.

Planner III, Maverick Yeh, reviewed Item 3.1: Project ZMA-26-002, a Zoning Map and General Plan
Amendment at 2193 East 6525 South. The request was to amend the land use designation from
Residential Rural Density to Residential Low Density and rezone the subject property from RR-1-21
to R-1-15 to create three single-family lots. The subject property is in an established single-family
residential neighborhood with existing utilities and roadway infrastructure and consisting of both
conforming and legal nonconforming lots.

The applicant’s neighborhood analysis identified the following:

   •   A total of 29 of the 57 lots (51%) were legal non-conforming.
   •   Many lots were smaller than the 21,000-square-foot minimum lot size required by the zone.
   •   The existing neighborhood contains varied lot widths and sizes.
   •   The proposed lots were generally consistent with portions of the surrounding development
       pattern.

Staff determined that the surrounding neighborhood had historically developed with a smaller lot
pattern than currently required under the RR-1-21 district. A Geographic Information Systems
(“GIS”) analysis found that 40 of the 63 lots in the study area (63.5%) are legal nonconforming and
do not meet one or more RR-1-21 dimensional standards, including minimum lot size and/or lot width
requirements.

Rural Residential zoning carries limited animal rights. Per Cottonwood Heights Municipal Code
(“CHMC”) §8.14.020, a minimum lot size of 20,000 square feet is required to keep livestock. Staff
analysis determined that existing neighborhood conditions differed from the original intent of the
zoning district, as 35 of the 63 surrounding lots (55.6%) do not meet this size requirement and cannot
utilize the livestock rights associated with the zone.

The subject property currently carries a land use designation of Residential Rural Density, which is
intended for lots 21,000 square feet or larger in size or approximately two dwelling units per acre.
The proposed designation of Residential Low-Density was intended for detached single-family homes
on lots between 8,700 and 17,400 square feet and between two-and-a-half and five units per acre.

Staff acknowledges that the request represented a departure from the historic intent of the Rural
Residential designation. However, the analysis determined the following:

   •   The existing neighborhood contains a mixture of conforming and legal non-conforming lots.
   •   The proposal maintains the detached single-family residential land use.
   •   The proposal does not introduce multi-family or commercial uses.
   •   The proposal may better align with the existing and anticipated development pattern of the
       neighborhood.

Mr. Yeh reviewed a concept rendering of the proposed development. The subject property would be
subdivided into three single-family lots, each approximately 0.36 acres in size.



Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                           2
Staff review of public services and infrastructure determined that:

   •   Existing roadway, water, and sewer service is available.
   •   Existing storm drainage infrastructure is available.
   •   Future development would remain subject to:
          o Subdivision review
          o Engineering review
          o Utility review
          o Fire Department review
          o Building permits

As Zoning Map and General Plan Map amendments are legislative actions, the Planning
Commission’s authority was to take public comment, discuss the merits of the proposal, and make a
recommendation to the City Council. The City Council was the final approval authority for the
application.

Public notice was mailed to all property owners within 1,000 feet of the subject property and posted
at the property in accordance with City and State Code requirements. One comment was received in
support of the application.

Staff recommended approval based on the following:

       1.      Compatible with the surrounding neighborhood.
       2.      Maintains low-density residential character.
       3.      Existing infrastructure is available.
       4.      Supports efficient use of serviced land.
       5.      No material impact on public health, safety, or welfare.

Commissioner Anderson asked about sidewalk and road improvements. Mr. Yeh reported that all
right-of-way improvements are reviewed during the subdivision process, but standard improvements
will be required. Commissioner Mills added that curb, gutter, and sidewalk are traditionally required
with this type of development, as it presents the opportunity for the City to bring older areas up to
current standards. Commissioner Anderson remarked that it would be the only sidewalk on that road.
Commissioner Mills encouraged the Commission to continue recommending sidewalks where
possible, as that is the only way the Fort Union Master Plan will be realized. The City does not have
money available to install sidewalks everywhere they are needed, so they need to be added a piece at
a time.

In response to a question from Commissioner Anderson, Mr. Yeh confirmed that the subject property
was currently an empty field. Commissioner Anderson stated that she visited the site, and it did not
look large enough for three homes. Commissioner Mills stated that he had the same question, but 96
feet is a good lot width, and a high-quality home can be built on an 0.33-acre lot.

Commissioner Anderson asked about the maximum amount of grass allowed for new development,
as the concept rendering showed all-grass yards. Mr. Yeh reported that no more than 35% grass is
allowed, and that will be verified during building permit review. In response to her follow-up



Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                          3
question, Mr. Spung reported that the next steps after approval would be subdivision and building
permit applications and review.

In response to a question from Commissioner Smith, Commissioner Mills stated that there is also a
limit on the percentage of impermeable surface allowed.

Chair Steinman asked if the Fire Department had any concerns about turnarounds or other aspects of
the proposal. Mr. Yeh reported that the Fire Department reviewed the proposal during the pre-
application meeting and is confident that there will be no issues. Mr. Spung added that there is a
hydrant near the property and an existing hammerhead in the public right-of-way. Fire Department
requirements are reviewed with the subdivision application.

Commissioner Mills asked Staff to be thoughtful about how to address the property near the Highland
Point Apartments.

Chair Steinman asked about the percentage of the City that was zoned agricultural, as the specific
zone no longer seemed to fit with the General Plan and there may be an opportunity to create an
overlay zone. Mr. Spung reported that most properties along Creek Road are zoned Rural Residential,
as are some parcels in southern Cottonwood Heights.

Item 3.2 was Project ADU-26-001. Mr. Yeh reported that the 0.30-acre subject property was located
at 2982 East 7375 South in the R-1-8 Zone. Site photographs and concept renderings were reviewed.
The proposed accessory dwelling unit (“ADU”) would be located in the rear yard, consistent with
ADU regulations, and the existing detached garage would be removed. The proposed two-bedroom
ADU was approximately 800 square feet in size and 10 to 15 feet tall, with a permanent foundation.
The structure would have 25-foot rear and eight-foot side setbacks as required by code.

The Site Plan was reviewed. In response to a question raised by Commissioner Mills, Mr. Yeh
clarified that per City Code, ADU parking cannot block parking for the primary structure. The owner
intended to remove the existing trees and a portion of the carport and extend the driveway to the front
of the ADU. Parking locations for each structure were identified on a street view image of the subject
property. Commissioner Mills expressed concern that the plan would require double-stacked parking
for the primary structure. Chair Steinman asked if additional pavement could be added to extend the
width of the driveway. Mr. Spung reported that the driveway could be widened by eight to nine feet,
and an average parking stall is nine feet wide.

In response to a question from Chair Steinman, Mr. Yeh clarified that the applicant intended to
remove a portion of the carport to extend the driveway. Staff was initially inclined to deny the
application, but the applicant was willing to modify the structure, remove a tree, and extend the
driveway to meet ADU parking standards. Those changes would be verified during building permit
review, but the Planning Commission could also require them as a condition of approval. Chair
Steinman stated that the City should be very clear about appropriate access to ADU parking.

In response to a question raised by Commissioner Anderson, it was clarified that there are no setback
requirements for parking; vehicles can park next to the property line.




Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                            4
Commissioner Mills asked if there were any existing easements in the area. Mr. Yeh reported that a

Item 3.3 was Project CUP-26-007. Mr. Spung reported that the request was for a Conditional Use
Permit (“CUP”) for the construction of a rectory at Saint John’s Anglican Church at 7136 South 1700
East. An existing structure previously served as a residence for clergy, but it is no longer habitable,
and they would like to replace it with a new residence. Pursuant to CHMC § 19.04.520, a rectory is
defined as: A place of residence for ministers, priests, nuns, or rabbis. The residence must be located
on the same parcel as the church and is considered an accessory use.

The Zoning Map, Site Plan, and site photographs were reviewed. The proposed structure was a single-
story home with five bedrooms, three bathrooms, a maximum height of 22 feet, and was designed to
complement both the church and the surrounding neighborhood. The residence will include an
attached two-car garage and a two-vehicle carport. It will function solely as a residence for clergy.
Per the applicant, redevelopment would improve the appearance and functionality of the property by
replacing a deteriorated structure and removing overgrown landscaping.

Staff analysis determined the following:

   •   City Code allows a rectory as a Conditional Use in the R-1-8 Zone, but does not provide
       specific development standards. Staff evaluated the project using applicable standards for a
       typical single-family home.
   •   The proposed rectory is a 3,270-square-foot, single-story residence reaching approximately
       22 feet in height, below the 35-foot maximum allowed in the zone.
   •   The proposed building meets or exceeds all required setbacks and is situated on a portion of
       the property that could function as a conforming residential lot under current zoning standards.
   •   The project provides four off-street parking spaces, which exceeds the minimum parking
       requirements for a single-family dwelling.

Commissioner Anderson asked if there would still be sufficient parking for the church. Mr. Spung
reported that the rectory parking will be separate and not impact church parking.

The Fire Department requested that a letter be obtained from Salt Lake City Public Utilities specifying
the available water flow from the nearest fire hydrant prior to building permit approval. If adequate
water flow is not available, the applicant may be required to upsize or install an additional hydrant.

       3.1       Project ZMA-26-002/GPA-26-002 – The Planning Commission will hold a public
                 hearing to review a zoning text amendment request initiated by Jordan Brady.
                 The Request to amend the General Plan Land Use designation from Rural
                 Residential to Residential Low Density and rezone approximately 1.08 acres at
                 2193 E. 6525 S. from RR-1-21 to R-1-15. The proposal is intended to facilitate
                 low-density residential infill development.

Mr. Yeh presented the Staff Report and indicated that the applicant, Jordan Brady on behalf of the
Brady Family Trust, had requested a Zoning Map and General Plan Amendment at 2193 East 6525
South. The request was to amend the General Plan land use designation from Residential Rural

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                        8
Density to Residential Low Density and rezone the subject property from RR-1-21 to R-1-15 to create
three single-family lots. Current and proposed Land Use and Zoning Maps were reviewed.

Existing conditions were as follows:

   •   The subject property is in an established single-family residential neighborhood.
   •   The property was currently zoned RR-1-21.
   •   Existing utilities and roadway infrastructure were available.
   •   The neighborhood consists of both conforming and legal non-conforming lots.

The applicant’s neighborhood analysis identified the following:

   •   A total of 29 of the 57 lots (51%) were legal non-conforming.
   •   Many lots were smaller than the 21,000-square-foot minimum lot size required by the zone.
   •   The existing neighborhood contains varied lot widths and sizes.
   •   The proposed lots were generally consistent with portions of the surrounding development
       pattern.

Staff conducted a Geographic Information Systems (“GIS”) analysis and found that 40 of the 63 lots
in the study area (63.5%) are legal nonconforming and do not meet one or more RR-1-21 dimensional
standards, including minimum lot size and/or lot width requirements.

Rural Residential zoning carries limited animal rights. Per CHMC § 8.14.020, a minimum lot size of
20,000 square feet is required to keep livestock. Staff analysis determined that 55.6% of surrounding
lots do not meet this size requirement and are therefore unable to fully utilize the livestock rights
associated with the zone.

The subject property currently carries a General Plan land use designation of Residential Rural
Density, which is intended for large-lot development. Lots must be 21,000 square feet or larger in
size, with a maximum of two dwelling units per acre. The proposed designation of Residential Low
Density was intended for detached single-family homes on lots between 8,700 and 17,400 square feet
and a maximum of five units per acre.

Staff acknowledged that the request represented a departure from the historic intent of the Rural
Residential designation. However, the analysis determined the following:

   •   The existing neighborhood contains a mixture of conforming and legal non-conforming lots.
   •   The proposal maintains the detached single-family residential land use.
   •   The proposal does not introduce multifamily or commercial uses.
   •   The proposal may better align with the existing and anticipated development pattern of the
       neighborhood.

Mr. Yeh reviewed a concept rendering of the proposed development. The subject property would be
subdivided into three single-family lots, each approximately 0.36 acres in size.

Staff review of public services and infrastructure determined that:


Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                          9
   •   Existing roadway, water, and sewer service is available.
   •   Existing storm drainage infrastructure is available.
   •   Future development would be subject to:
          o Subdivision review
          o Engineering review
          o Utility review
          o Fire Department review
          o Building permits

As Zoning Map and General Plan Map amendments are legislative actions, the Planning
Commission’s authority was to take public comment, discuss the merits of the proposal, and make a
recommendation to the City Council. The City Council had final approval authority.

Public notice was mailed to all property owners within 1,000 feet of the subject property and posted
at the property in accordance with City and State Code requirements. One comment was received in
support of the application.

Staff recommended approval based on the following:

       1.      Compatible with surrounding neighborhood.
       2.      Maintains low-density residential character.
       3.      Existing infrastructure is available.
       4.      Supports efficient use of serviced land.
       5.      No material impact on public health, safety, or welfare.

The applicant, Jordan Brady, reported that he and his wife, Brooke, had lived in Cottonwood Heights
for six years and rented a property owned by the Brady Family Trust. They had five children in
Cottonwood Heights schools. His hope was that everyone would make informed decisions, and the
Work Session gave him confidence as everyone was prepared and had reviewed Mr. Yeh’s report and
his application.

In preparation for the meeting, they spoke with as many neighboring homeowners as possible.
Concerns they raised included increased, traffic and water use, as well as the potential need to upgrade
the fire truck turnaround. Their research determined the following:

   •   Traffic: The average trips per residence is 9.5 to 10, so the three proposed lots would result in
       an approximately 5% increase in traffic on 6525 South.
   •   Water: Lots in the current RR-1-21 Zone typically require almost twice as much water use as
       the proposed R-1-15 Zone, primarily due to the amount of impermeable surface. The proposal
       would create three lots but only increase water use by between 15% and 20% in comparison
       to the existing lot.
   •   Fire: He met with the Fire Marshall at the property, who confirmed that the existing
       hammerhead turnaround meets the standards required by City ordinance. He did not mention
       the need to pave the road.

Mr. Brady believed the proposal would benefit the community as it would add thoughtfully designed
housing in a high-demand area, support efficient land use and sustainability goals, develop an


Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                            10
undeveloped property, and reinforce planned development that enhances the community’s character.
There would be no displacement or infringement on homeowners’ animal rights, and the property
would conform to the spirit and intent of the General Plan and provide a balance between existing
zoning and the actual character of the neighborhood.

City was not interested in flippers, and Commissioner Mills would not facilitate an investment
property in a neighborhood that is already struggling. He was also concerned about the parking
situation. Existing parking should be preserved, and tandem parking should not be allowed, which
would require two parking stalls at the rear with clear ingress and egress.

In response to a question from Commissioner Lugo, Chair Steinman clarified that ADU standards
prohibit the property owner from renting out the primary residence. Commissioner Lugo stated that
the application needed to be resubmitted if the property owner moved back into the home.

Commissioner Mills moved to DENY Project ADU-26-001 based on questions related to the
applicant’s current housing circumstance. Commissioner Anderson seconded the motion. Vote
on Motion: Commissioner Barnes-Yes; Commissioner Anderson-Yes; Commissioner Smith-Yes;
Commissioner Mills-Yes; Commissioner Lugo-Yes; Chair Steinman-Yes. The motion passed
unanimously.

       3.3     Project CUP-26-007 – The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to
               review and take possible action on a request for approval of a Conditional Use
               Permit to construct a rectory accessory to the existing church located at 7136
               South 1700 East. The proposed rectory will provide residential housing for clergy
               associated with the church.

Mr. Spung reported that the request was for a CUP for the construction of a rectory at Saint John’s
Anglican Church at 7136 South 1700 East to serve as a residence for onsite clergy. An existing
structure is no longer habitable, and they would like to replace it with a new residence.

Pursuant to CHMC § 19.04.520, a rectory is defined as: A place of residence for ministers, priests,
nuns, or rabbis and requires a CUP in the R-1-8 Zone. The residence must be located on the same
parcel as the church and is considered an accessory use.

The Zoning Map, Site Plan, and site photographs were reviewed. The proposed structure was a single-
story home with five bedrooms, three bathrooms, a maximum height of 22 feet, and was designed to
complement both the church and the surrounding neighborhood. The residence will include an
attached two-car garage and a two-vehicle carport. It will function solely as a residence for clergy.


Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 06/03/26                                             16
Per the applicant, redevelopment will improve the appearance and functionality of the property by
replacing a deteriorated structure and removing overgrown landscaping.

City Code allows a rectory as a Conditional Use in the R-1-8 Zone, but does not provide specific
development standards. Staff evaluated the project using applicable standards for a typical single-
family home, and those requirements were met. The Fire Department requested that a letter be
obtained from Salt Lake City Public Utilities confirming available water flow from the nearest fire
hydrant prior to issuance of a building permit. The Engineering Department did not have concerns.

Notices were posted and mailed to property owners within 300 feet of the subject property at least 10
days in advance of the meeting. No comments were received.

Staff recommended approval subject to the modified Conditions of Approval as read during the Work
Session.

Chair Steinman opened the public hearing. There were no comments. The public hearing was closed.

Commissioner Lugo stated that any time the Planning Commission has the opportunity to enhance
real estate in Cottonwood Heights, they should do so. He attended this church in the 1980s and 1990s,
and it was great to see it being improved.

Chair Steinman congratulated the applicant on the donation of the church. It is exciting to see that
happen as it shows the motives and passion of the community.

Commissioner Mills stated that it would be helpful to specifically call out the lighting ordinance, but
that would likely be handled during the building permit process. Mr. Yeh confirmed that a lighting
plan is required with the building permit application and is reviewed for compliance with the lighting
ordinance.

Commissioner Anderson moved to APPROVE Project CUP-26-007 based on the findings and
recommendations listed in the Staff Report dated June 3, 2026, and subject to the conditions listed
therein. Commissioner Barnes seconded the motion. Vote on Motion: Commissioner Barnes-Yes;
Commissioner Anderson-Yes; Commissioner Smith-Yes; Commissioner Mills-Yes; Commissioner
Lugo-Yes; Chair Steinman-Yes. The motion passed unanimously.
